92\begin{document}
93\title{A Categorical Outlook on Cellular Automata}
94\author{S. Capobianco}{Silvio Capobianco}
95\author{T. Uustalu}{Tarmo Uustalu}
96\address{Institute of Cybernetics at Tallinn University of Technology \\
97Akadeemia tee 21\\ 12618 Tallinn, Estonia}
98\email{{silvio, tarmo}@cs.ioc.ee}
99\thanks{This research was supported by the European Regional
100Development Fund (ERDF) through the Estonian Center of Excellence in
101Computer Science (EXCS) and by the Estonian Science Foundation under
102grant no.~6940.}
103\begin{abstract}\noindent
104In programming language semantics, it has proved to be fruitful to
105analyze context-dependent notions of computation, e.g., dataflow
106computation and attribute grammars, using comonads. We explore the
107viability and value of similar modeling of cellular automata. We
108identify local behaviors of cellular automata with coKleisli maps of
109the exponent comonad on the category of uniform spaces and uniformly
110continuous functions and exploit this equivalence to conclude some
111standard results about cellular automata as instances of basic
112category-theoretic generalities. In particular, we recover
113Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert's version of the Curtis-Hedlund
114theorem.
115\end{abstract}
116\maketitle
117\section{Introduction}
118Since the seminal work of Moggi~\cite{m91}, it has become standard in
119programming language semantics to analyze functions producing effects
120such as exceptions, input, output, interactive input-output,
121nondeterminism, probabilistic choice, state, continuations using
122monads. Specifically, effectful functions are identified with Kleisli
123maps of a suitable monad on the category of pure functions.
124Wadler~\cite{w92} put this view to further use in programming
125methodology by extracting from it a very useful programming idiom for
126purely functional languages like Haskell.
127The dual view of context-dependent functions as coKleisli maps of a
128comonad is equally useful, but less well known. Brookes and Geva
129\cite{bg92} explained the ``intensional'' aspect of denotational
130semantics in terms of the $\omega$-chain comonad on the category of
131$\omega$-cpos. More recently, Uustalu and Vene \cite{uv06,uv07,uv08}
132employed comonads to analyze dataflow computation and attribute
133grammars and Hasuo et al.~\cite{hju07} treated tree transducers.
134Characteristic of many context-dependent notions of computation is
135shape-preserving transformation of some datastructure based on a value
136update rule which is local in nature and applied uniformly to every
137node. This is the case with dataflow computation where such a
138transformation is applied to a list or to a stream with a
139distinguished position and with attribute grammars where computation
140happens on a tree or a tree with a distinguished position (a
141``zipper''). Cellular automata are similar, the datastructure being
142the integer line or plane or, more generally, a group. It should
143therefore be worthwhile to test the slogan that context-dependent
144computation is comonadic also on cellular automata. To a degree, this
145has already been done, as Piponi~\cite{p06} programmed cellular
146automata in Haskell using the comonadic interface. However, he did not
147use his modeling of cellular automata to prove properties about them
148and also dropped the classical requirement that cellular automata rely
149on a finite neighborhood only.
150In this paper, we study the comonadic aspect of cellular automata
151deeper. We identify cellular automata (more exactly their local
152behaviors) with coKleisli maps of the exponent monad on $\Unif$, the
153category of uniform spaces and uniformly continuous functions, and
154explore whether this view can be useful. We see that it is: we can
155conclude some standard results about cellular automata as instances of
156category-theoretic generalities. In particular, we recover the
157Curtis-Hedlund theorem~\cite{h69}---a characterization of global
158behaviors of cellular automata---in the version of
159Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert~\cite{csc08} (this applies to
160general discrete alphabets rather than finite alphabets only). This
161theorem turns out to be an instance of the basic category-theoretic
162fact that the coKleisli category of a comonad is isomorphic to the
163full subcategory of its co-Eilenberg-Moore category given by the
164cofree coalgebras. We also show that the comonadic view allows one to
165see 2-dimensional cellular automata as 1-dimensional and treat
166point-dependent cellular automata.
167The paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:com} is a quick
168introduction to comonads while Section~\ref{sec:top} reviews some
169preliminaries about topological and uniform spaces. In
170Section~\ref{sec:ca}, we show that cellular automata local behaviors
171are the same as coKleisli maps of a certain comonad. In
172Section~\ref{sec:ch}, we recover the Curtis-Hedlund theorem (in the
173version of Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert). In
174Section~\ref{sec:rev}, we reprove the reversibility principle. In
175Sections~\ref{sec:2d}, \ref{sec:dep}, we discuss some further
176applications of the comonadic view: 2-dimensional cellular automata as
1771-dimensional and point-dependent cellular automata.
178The paper assumes knowledge of basic category theory (categories,
179functors, natural transformations, Cartesian closed categories), but
180is self-contained in regards to comonads. For background material on
181category theory and (co)monads in particular, we refer the reader to
182Barr and Wells~\cite[Ch.~1, 3]{bw83}. We also assume the basics of
183\ca\ as presented by Ceccherini-Silberstein and
184Coornaert~\cite[Ch.~1]{csc10}.

188\section{Comonads}
189\label{sec:com}
190Given two categories $\C$, $\D$ and a functor $L : \D \to \C$, a
191\emph{right adjoint} to $L$ is given by a functor $R : \C \to \D$ and
192two natural transformations $\eps : LR \to \Id_\C$ (the \emph{counit})
193and $\eta : \Id_\D \to RL$ (the \emph{unit}) such that the diagrams
194\[
195\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
196L \ar[r]^{L \eta} \ar@{=}[dr]
197& LRL \ar[d]^{\eps L} \\
198& L
199}
200\hspace*{1cm}
201\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
202R \ar[d]_{\eta R} \ar@{=}[dr]
203& \\
204RLR \ar[r]_{R \eps}
205& R
206}
207\]
208commute. Equivalently, a right adjoint may be given by an object
209mapping $R : |\C| \to |\D|$, for any object $A \in |\C|$, a map
210$\eps_A : LRA \to A$, and, for any objects $A \in |\D|$, $B \in |\C|$
211and map $k : LA \to B$, a map $k^\ddg : A \to RB$ (the \emph{right
212transpose}) such that
213\begin{itemize}
214\item for any objects $A \in |\D|$, $B \in |\C|$, and map $k : LA \to
215B$, $\eps_B \comp L k^\ddg = k$,
216\item for any object $A \in |\C|$, $(\eps_A)^\ddg = \id_{R A}$,
217\item for any objects $A, B \in |\D|$, $C \in |\C|$ and maps $f : A
218\to B$, $k : L B \to C$, $(k \comp L f)^\ddg = k^\ddg \comp f$.
219\end{itemize}
220The morphism mapping part of $R$ and unit $\eta$ define the right
221transpose of $k : LA \to B$ by $k^\ddg \eqdf R k \comp \eta_A$. The
222right transpose $(-)^\ddg$ determines the morphism mapping part of $R$
223and unit $\eta$ by $R f \eqdf (f \comp \eps_A)^\ddg$, for $f : A \to
224B$, and $\eta_A \eqdf (\id_{LA})^\ddg$.
225A \emph{comonad} on a category $\C$ is given by a functor $D : \C \to
226\C$ and natural transformations $\eps : D \to \Id_\C$ (the \emph{counit})
227and $\de : D \to DD$ (the \emph{comultiplication}) making the diagrams
228\[
229\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
230D \ar[r]^{\de} \ar[d]_{\de} \ar@{=}[rd]
231& DD \ar[d]^{\eps D} \\
232DD \ar[r]^{D\eps} & D
233}
234\hspace*{1cm}
235\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
236D \ar[r]^-{\de} \ar[d]_{\de} & DD \ar[d]^{\de D} \\
237DD \ar[r]^-{D\de} & DDD
238}
239\]
240commute. Equivalently, a comonad can be given by an object mapping $D
241: |\C| \to |\C|$, for any object $A \in |\C|$, a map $\eps_A : DA \to
242A$, and, for any objects $A, B \in |\C|$ and map $k : DA \to B$, a map
243$k^\dg : DA \to DB$ (the \emph{coKleisli extension}) such that
244\begin{itemize}
245\item for any objects $A, B \in |\C|$ and map $k : DA \to B$, $\eps_B
246\comp k^\dg = k$,
247\item for any object $A$, $(\eps_A)^\dg = \id_{D A}$,
248\item for any objects $A, B, C \in |\C|$ and maps $k : DA \to B$,
249$\ell : D B \to C$, $(\ell \comp k^\dg)^\dg = \ell^\dg \comp k^\dg$.
250\end{itemize}
251The morphism mapping part of $D$ and comultiplication $\de$ define the
252coKleisli extension $(-)^\dg$ by $k^\dg \eqdf D k \comp \de_A$.
253Conversely, the $(-)^\dg$ determines the morphism mapping part of $D$ and
254comultiplication $\de$ by $D f \eqdf (f \comp \eps_A)^\dg$, $\de_A
255\eqdf (\id_{D A})^\dg$.
256A functor $L : \C \to \D$ with a right adjoint $(R, \eps, \eta)$,
257defines a comonad on $\C$ with counit $\eps$ by $D \eqdf LR$, $\de
258\eqdf L\eta R$, alternatively by $D A \eqdf L (R A)$, $k^\dg \eqdf L
259k^\ddg$.
260In the converse direction, a comonad $(D, \eps, \de)$ on $\C$ induces
261a whole category of adjunctions $(\D, L, R, \eta)$ that have $\eps$ as
262the counit and satisfy $D = LR$, $\de = L \eta R$, called
263\emph{splittings} of the comonad. This category has initial and final
264objects, which are known as the coKleisli and coEilenberg-Moore
265splittings of the comonad.
266The \emph{coKleisli category} $\coKl(D)$ has as objects those of $\C$
267and as maps from $A$ to $B$ those from $DA$ to $B$ of $\C$. The
268identity $\idD_A$ on object $A$ is defined by $\idD_A \eqdf \eps_A$.
269The composition $\ell \compD k$ of maps $k : DA \to B$ and $\ell : DB
270\to C$ is $\ell \compD k \eqdf \ell \comp D k \comp \de_A = \ell
271\comp k^\dg$. The functor $L : \coKl(D) \to \C$ in the coKleisli
272splitting is defined by $L A \eqdf D A$, $L k \eqdf k^\dg$. The right
273adjoint, unit and right transpose are defined by $R A \eqdf A$, $R f
274\eqdf f \comp \eps_A$, $\eta_A \eqdf \id_{D A}$, $k^\ddg \eqdf k$.
275The \emph{coEilenberg-Moore category} $\coEM(D)$ has as objects
276coalgebras of $D$ and as maps coalgebra maps of $D$. A
277\emph{coalgebra} of $D$ is given by an object $A \in |\C|$ and map $u
278: A \to DA$ (the \emph{coalgebra structure}) making the diagrams
279\[
280\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
281A \ar[r]^{u} \ar@{=}[rd]
282& DA \ar[d]^{\eps_A} \\
283& A
284}
285\hspace*{1cm}
286\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
287A \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_{u} & DA \ar[d]^{\de_A} \\
288DA \ar[r]^-{D u} & D(DA)
289}
290\]
291commute. A \emph{coalgebra map}
292between $(A, u)$ and $(B, v)$ is a map $f : A \to B$ making the
293diagram
294\[
295\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
296A \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_{f}
297& DA \ar[d]^{D f} \\
298B \ar[r]^-{v}
299& DB
300}
301\]
302commute. The identity and composition are inherited from $\C$. The
303functor $L : \coEM(D) \to \C$ in the splitting of $D$ through
304$\coEM(D)$ is the coalgebra-structure forgetful functor: $L (A, u)
305\eqdf A$, $L f \eqdf f$. The right adjoint $R$ is defined by $R A
306\eqdf (D A, \de_A)$, $R f \eqdf D f$. The unit and right transpose are
307defined by $\eta_{(A,u)} \eqdf u$ and $k^\ddg \eqdf D k \comp u$ (for
308$k : L (A, u) \to B)$.
309The functor $R$ being the right adjoint of the forgetful functor
310implies that
311, for any $B$, the coalgebra $R B = (D B, \de_B)$ is the cofree coalgebra on $B$, i.e.,
312for any coalgebra $(A, u)$, object $B$
313and map $k : A \to B$, there is a unique map $f : A \to D B$, namely
314$k^\ddg$, such that the diagrams
315\[
316\xymatrix@R=1.8pc{
317& A \ar[dl]_{k} \ar[r]^-{u} \ar@{.>}[d]^{f} & DA \ar@{.>}[d]^{Df} \\
318B & DB \ar[l]_{\eps_B} \ar[r]^-{\de_B} & D(DB)
319}
320\]
321commute.
322The unique splitting map between the coKleisli and coEilenberg-Moore
323splitting is the functor $E : \coKl(D) \to \coEM(D)$ defined by $E A
324\eqdf (D A, \de_A)$, $E k \eqdf D k \comp \de_A = k^\dg$. This functor
325is a full embedding. The image of $E$ is the full subcategory of
326$\coEM(D)$ given by the cofree coalgebras that is therefore isomorphic
327to $\coKl(D)$.
328A simple and instructive example of a comonad and its coKleisli and
329coEilenberg-Moore splittings is given by the \emph{reader} (or
330\emph{product}) \emph{comonad}. It is defined on any category $\C$
331with finite products, but let us choose $\C$ to be $\Set$ (or $\Top$
332or $\Unif$), so we can write pointwise definitions for intuitiveness.
333Given some fixed object $C \in |\C|$, it is defined by $D A \eqdf A
334\times C$, $D f (x, c) \eqdf (f (x), c)$, $\eps_A (x, c) \eqdf x$,
335$\de_A (x, c) \eqdf ((x, c), c)$, $k^\dg (x, c) \eqdf (k (x, c), c)$.
336The coKleisli category has as objects those of $\C$ and as maps from
337$A$ to $B$ those from $A \times C$ to $B$. The identities and
338composition are defined by $\idD (x, c) \eqdf x$, $(\ell \compD k)
339(x, c) \eqdf \ell(k (x, c), c)$.
340A coalgebra of $D$ is given by an object $A$ and a map $u : A \to A
341\times C$ satisfying the laws of a coalgebra. Let us define
342$(u_0(x), u_1(x)) \eqdf u(x)$. The laws impose that
343$u_0(x) = x$ and $((u_0(x),u_1(x)), u_1(x)) =
344(u(u_0(x)),u_1(x))$.
345The first law defines $u_0$ and the second becomes a tautology as soon as this definition is substituted into it.
346Hence,
347a coalgebra is effectively the same as an object $A$ with an unconstrained map $u_1 : A \to C$.
348A map between $D$-coalgebras $(A, u)$, $(B, v)$ is a map $f : A
349\to B$ such that $(f(u_0(x)),u_1(x)) = (v_0(f(x)),
350v_1(f(x)))$, which boils down to $u_1(x) = v_1(f(x))$.
351The coEilenberg-Moore category has thus as objects pairs of an object
352$A$ and map $u_1 : A \to C$ and a map between $(A, u_1)$, $(B, v_1)$
353is map $f : A \to B$ such that $u_1(x) = v_1(f(x))$. The cofree
354coalgebra on $A$ is the pair $(A \times C, {\delta_1}_A)$ where
355${\delta_1}_A (x, c) \eqdf c$.
356The isomorphism between $\coKl(D)$ and the category of cofree
357$D$-coalgebras establishes a 1-1 correspondence between maps $k :
358A \times C \to B$ and maps $f : A \times C \to B \times C$ such that
359${\delta_1}_B (f (x, c)) = c$.

363\section{Exponentials, topologies, and uniformities}
364\label{sec:top}
365Given an object $C$ in a category $\C$ with finite products, it is
366said to be \emph{exponentiable} if the functor $(-) \times C$ has a
367right adjoint. This amounts to the existence, for any object $A$, of an
368object $A^C$ (the \emph{exponential}) and map $\mathsf{ev}_A : A^C
369\times A \to C$ (the \emph{evaluation}) as well as, for any
370objects $A$, $B$ and map $k : A \times C \to B$, a map
371$\mathsf{cur}(k) : A \to B^C$ (the \emph{currying} of $k$) satisfying
372appropriate conditions. If every object of $\C$ is exponentiable, it is
373called \emph{Cartesian closed}. Intuitively, exponentials are
374internalized homsets. In $\Set$, every object $C$ is exponentiable and
375the exponential $A^C$ is the set of all functions from $C$ to $A$.
376Things are somewhat more complicated in the category $\Top$ of
377topological spaces, as the exponential $A^C$ is to be the set of
378continuous functions from $C$ to $A$, but it must also be given a
379topology. Moreover, the evaluation $\mathsf{ev}_A : A^C \times A \to
380C$ must be continuous and the currying $\mathsf{cur}(k) : A \to B^C$
381of a continuous function must be continuous.
382Not every topological space is exponentiable.
383Hausdorff spaces are exponentiable
384if and only if
385they are locally compact: in this case, the exponential topology on the space of continuous functions from $C$ to $A$ is the \emph{compact-open topology} generated by the sets $\{f : C \to A \mid f(K)\subseteq U\}$ with $K$ compact in $C$
386and $U$ open in $A$~\cite{eh01,g85}.
387In particular, discrete spaces are exponentiable (which also
388follows from
389the discrete topology making every function from it continuous)
390and their compact-open topology is in fact the product topology.
391That not all objects can act as exponents
392is also true in the category $\Unif$ of uniform spaces
393whose constituents we now define.
394A \emph{uniform space} is a set $A$ endowed with a \emph{uniformity},
395i.e., a collection $\mathcal{U}$
396of binary relations on $A$
397(called \emph{entourages})
398satisfying the following properties:
399\begin{enumerate}
400\item
401$\Delta\subseteq U$ for every $U\in\mathcal{U}$,
402where $\Delta=\{(x,x)\mid x\in A\}$
403is the \emph{diagonal}.
404\item
405If
406$U\subseteq V$
407and
408$U\in\mathcal{U}$
409then $V\in\mathcal{U}$.
410\item
411If $U,V\in\mathcal{U}$ then $U\cap V\in\mathcal{U}$.
412\item
413If $U\in\mathcal{U}$ then $U^{-1}\in\mathcal{U}$.
414\item
415If $U\in\mathcal{U}$ then
416\begin{math}
417V^2=\left\{
418(x,y) \mid \exists z \mid (x,z),(z,y) \in V
419\right\}\subseteq U
420\end{math}
421for some $V\in\mathcal{U}$.
422\end{enumerate}
423The simplest non-trivial uniformity on $A$
424is the \emph{discrete uniformity},
425made of all the supersets of the diagonal.
426A uniformity induces a topology as follows: $\Omega \subseteq A$ is open
427if and only if,
428for every $x \in \Omega$,
429there exists $U \in \mathcal{U}$ such that
430\begin{math}
431\{y\in A\mid(x,y)\in U\} \subseteq \Omega.
432\end{math}
433Such topology is Hausdorff if and only if
434\begin{math}
435\bigcap_{U\in\mathcal{U}}U=\Delta.
436\end{math}
437The discrete uniformity induces the discrete topology,
438but is not the only one that does (cf.~\cite[I-5]{i64}),
439i.e., uniform spaces may be discrete
440without being \emph{uniformly discrete}.
441A map $f : A \to B$ between uniform spaces
442is \emph{uniformly continuous} (briefly, u.c.)\
443if, for every entourage $V$ on $B$,
444there is an entourage $U$ on $A$ such that $(f \times f)(U) \subseteq V$.
445Any u.c.\ function is continuous
446in the topology induced by the uniformities:
447the converse is true if $A$ is compact~\cite[II-24]{i64}
448but false in general even for metric spaces.
449The \emph{product uniformity} is the coarsest uniformity
450that makes the projections uniformly continuous:
451the topology induced by the product uniformity is the product topology.
452A product of discrete uniformities is called \emph{prodiscrete}.
453In $\Unif$, uniformly discrete objects are exponentiable \cite[III.19
454and III.21]{i64}. Again, the reason is that every function from $C$ is
455u.c.\ as soon as $C$ is uniformly discrete.

459\section{Cellular automata as coKleisli maps}
460\label{sec:ca}
461Classically, a \emph{cellular automaton} on a monoid $(G, 1_G, \cdot)$
462(the \emph{universe})\footnote{Instead of the monoid, one usually
463takes a group in the cellular automata literature. But we do not
464need inverses in this paper.} and set $A$ (the
465\emph{alphabet})\footnote{The alphabet is
466often required to be finite. We make this assumption only where we need it.} is given by a finite subset $N$ of $G$ (the
467\emph{support neighborhood}) and function $d : A^N\to A$
468(the \emph{transition rule}).
469Any cellular automaton induces a \emph{local behavior} $k : A^G \to
470A$ via $k(c) \eqdf d (\restrict{c}{N})$.
471One speaks of elements $A^N$ of finite subsets $N \subseteq
472G$ as \emph{patterns} and elements of $A^G$ as \emph{configurations}.
473Transition rules work on patterns, local behaviors on configurations.
474Cellular automata that induce the same local behavior are considered
475equivalent. In this paper, we will not distinguish between equivalent
476cellular automata, hence we can identify cellular automata with their
477local behaviors.
478If the alphabet $A$ is finite, a function $k : A^G \to A$ is a local
479behavior (i.e., the local behavior of some cellular automaton) if and
480only if it is continuous for the discrete topology on $A$ and the
481product topology on $A^G$.
482In the general case (where $A$ may be infinite), the above equivalence
483does not generally hold, but a refinement does. A function $k : A^G
484\to A$ is then a local behavior iff it is uniformly continuous for the
485discrete uniformity on $A$ and product uniformity on $A^G$.\footnote{
486(Cf.~\cite[Th. 1.9.1]{csc10})
487Every entourage of the prodiscrete uniformity
488contains an entourage of the form
489\begin{math}
490V_N = \left\{
491(c,e)
492\mid \restrict{c}{N} = \restrict{e}{N}
493\right\}
494\end{math}
495with $N \subseteq G$ finite.
496If $k : A^G \to A$ is u.c.\ with $A$ uniformly discrete, then
497$(k \times k)(V_N) \subseteq \Delta$ for some finite $N \subseteq G$:
498thus, $k(c)$ only depends on $\restrict{c}{N}$.
499}
500The finite case becomes an instance: if $A$ is finite, then $A^G$ is compact and therefore any
501continuous function $k : A^G \to A$ is uniformly continuous.
502Based on these observations, we henceforth take it as a definition
503that a local behavior on a set (the alphabet) $A$ is a uniformly
504continuous function $k : A^G \to A$ wrt.\ the prodiscrete uniformity on
505$A^G$ and forget about the definition of cellular automata in terms of
506a support neighborhood and a transition rule.
507Any local behavior $k$ induces a \emph{global behavior} $k^\dg : A^G
508\to A^G$, a map between configurations, via
509$
510k^\dg (c)(x) \eqdf k (c \rhd x)
511$
512where $\rhd : A^G \times G \to A^G$ (the \emph{translation} of
513configurations) is defined by
514$
515(c \rhd x)(y) \eqdf c(x \cdot y)
516$
517The translation is a uniformly continuous function. It follows that
518the global behavior $k^\dg$ is also uniformly continuous.
519Local behaviors on a fixed universe $G$ and fixed alphabet $A$ form a
520monoid with unit $\idD$ given by $\idD (c) \eqdf c (1_G)$ and
521multiplication $\bullet$ given by $\ell \compD k \eqdf \ell \comp
522k^\dg$. Indeed, it is easy to see that $\idD$ is uniformly continuous
523and $\compD$ preserves uniform continuity (because $(-)^\dg$ does) and
524the monoid laws turn out to hold too.
525We now make two small generalizations and make a richer category out
526of local behaviors: after all, a monoid is a category with one
527object. First, we do not insist that the alphabet be a discrete
528uniform space, it may be any uniform space. And second, we give up
529the idea of a fixed alphabet: we let the local behavior change the
530alphabet.
531For a fixed monoid $G$ (the universe), we redefine a \emph{local
532behavior} between two general uniform spaces (the source and target
533alphabets) $A$ and $B$ to be a uniformly continuous function $k : A^G
534\to B$ where $A^G$ is given the product uniformity.
535Local behaviors now make a category that has as objects alphabets and
536as maps local behaviors between them. The identity on $A$ is $\idD_A
537: A^G \to A$ given by $\idD_A (c) \eqdf c (1_G)$ and the composition
538$\ell \compD k : A^G \to C$ of two maps $k : A^G \to B$ and $\ell :
539B^G \to C$ given by $\ell \compD k \eqdf \ell \comp k^\dg$ where
540$k^\dg : A^G \to B^G$ is defined by $k^\dg(c)(x) \eqdf k(c \rhd_A x)$
541from $\rhd_A : A^G \times G \to A^G$ defined by $(c \rhd_A x)(y) \eqdf
542c(x \cdot y)$. Notice that these definitions coincide exactly with
543those we made for the monoid of local behaviors above, except that
544local behaviors can now mediate between different alphabets that need
545not be uniformly discrete. The function $\idD_A$ is still uniformly
546continuous for any $A$ and the operation $\compD$ preserves uniform
547continuity.
548While the generalized definition of local behaviors is more liberal
549than the classical one, it is conservative over it in the following
550sense: The local behaviors from any uniformly discrete space $A$ back
551to itself are exactly the classical local behaviors on $A$ seen as a
552set.
553We will now recover our category of local behaviors from a categorical
554generality, by showing that it is a straightforward instance of the
555coKleisli construction for a comonad.
556Any fixed monoid $(G, 1_G, \cdot)$ determines a comonad $(D, \eps,
557\delta)$ on $\Unif$ (in fact, on any category where the carrier $G$ is
558exponentiable, so also, e.g., on $\Set$ and $\Top$) (the
559\emph{cellular automata} or \emph{exponent} \emph{comonad}) as
560follows. The object mapping part of $D$ is defined by $D A \eqdf A^G$,
561where $A^G$ is the $G$-exponential of $A$, i.e., the space of uniformly
562continuous functions from $G$ to $A$ equipped with the prodiscrete
563uniformity. The morphism mapping part is defined by $D f \eqdf f^G$,
564i.e., $D f (c) \eqdf f \comp c$. The components of the counit $\eps_A
565: A^G \to A$ and comultiplication $\de_A : A^G \to (A^G)^G$ are
566defined by $\eps_A (c) \eqdf c(1_G)$ and $\de_A (c)(x) \eqdf c \rhd_A
567x$ (so that $\de_A (c) (x) (y) = c(x \cdot y)$); these functions are
568uniformly continuous. The general definition of the coKleisli
569extension $(-)^\dg$ via the morphism mapping part of $D$ and
570comultiplication $\de$ tells us that $k^\dg (c)(x) = D k (\de_A(c))(x)
571= k (\de_A(c)(x)) = k (c \rhd_A x)$.
572The laws of a comonad are proved from the monoid laws for $G$ by the
573following calculations (we omit the proofs of the naturality
574conditions of $\eps$ and $\de$).
575\[
576\begin{array}{c}
577\eps_{DA} (\de_A (c)) (x)
578= \de_A(c) (1_G) (x)
579= c (1_G \cdot x)
580= c(x)
581\\[1ex]
582c (x)
583= c (x \cdot 1_G)
584= \de_A (c) (x) (1_G)
585= \eps_A (\de_A (c) (x))
586= D\eps_A (\de_A (c)) (x)
587\\[1ex]
588\de_{DA} (\de_A (c)) (x) (y) (z)
589= \de_A(c) (x \cdot y) (z)
590= c ((x \cdot y) \cdot z)
591\hspace*{5cm} \\ \hspace*{1cm}
592= c (x \cdot (y \cdot z))
593= \de_A (c) (x) (y \cdot z)
594= \de_A (\de_A (c) (x)) (y) (z)
595= D\de_A (\de_A (c)) (x) (y) (z)
596\end{array}
597\]
598As we have seen, a comonad on a category always defines two canonical
599splittings of its underlying functor into two adjoint functors. The
600coKleisli splitting of our comonad $D$ on $\Unif$ goes via the
601coKleisli category which has as objects those of $\Unif$ and as maps
602from $A$ to $B$ those from $D A$ to $B$ in $\Unif$. The identity on
603$A$ is $\idD_A \eqdf \eps_A$ and the composition of $k$ and $\ell$ is
604$\ell \compD k \eqdf \ell \comp k^\dg$. Note that these are exactly
605the data of the category of local behaviors that we introduced above.
606But this time we do not have to prove that the unital and
607associativity laws of the category hold. Our proof obligations went
608into establishing that the comonad data are well defined and the comonad
609laws hold.

611% =======================================================================
612% =======================================================================
613\section{Retrieving the Curtis-Hedlund theorem}
614\label{sec:ch}
615Let $(D, \eps, \de)$ be the $G$-exponential comonad on $\Unif$ for a
616given monoid $(G, 1_G, \cdot)$, with $G$ endowed with the discrete
617uniformity, as introduced in the previous section.
618As we know from Section~\ref{sec:com}, $\coKl(D)$
619is equivalent to
620the category of cofree $D$-coalgebras under a comparison functor $E$ that sends a coKleisli map (local behavior) $k : D A \to B$ to the cofree coalgebra map $k^\dg : (D A, \de_A) \to (D B, \de_B)$, which, as a map of $\Unif$, we know to be the corresponding global behavior.
621Hence,
622a map $f : D A \to D B$ would be a global behavior if and only if $f$ is a cofree coalgebra map.
623Now, given an arbitrary comonad, it is usually of interest to study
624its general coalgebras and not only the cofree ones. We too
625follow this thumb rule.
626By definition, objects in $\coEM(D)$ are pairs of objects $A$ and maps
627$u:A\to DA$ in $\Unif$ satisfying
628\[
629\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
630A \ar[r]^-{u} \ar@{=}[rd] & A^G \ar[d]^{\eps_A} \\
631& A
632}
633\hspace*{1cm}
634\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
635A \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_{u} & A^G \ar[d]^{\de_A} \\
636A^G \ar[r]^-{u^G} & (A^G)^G
637}
638\]
639In our case,
640the first equation simply means
641\begin{math}
642u(a)(1_G)=a
643\end{math}
644while the second one simplifies to
645\begin{math}
646u(a)(x\cdot y)=u(u(a)(x))(y).
647\end{math}
648This writing, however, is cumbersome and unexplicative.
649To see more, we uncurry
650\begin{math}
651u:A\to A^G
652\end{math}
653to
654\begin{math}
655\otimes:A\times G\to A,
656\end{math}
657so that
658\begin{math}
659a \otimes x=u(a)(x).
660\end{math}
661Then the two equations become
662\begin{math}
663a\otimes 1_G=a,
664\end{math}
665and
666\begin{math}
667a\otimes (x\cdot y)=(a\otimes x)\otimes y.
668\end{math}
669Diagrammatically, this is to require commutation of
670\[
671\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
672A \ar[r]^-{\rho_A} \ar@{=}[rrd]
673& A \times 1 \ar[r]^-{A \times 1_G} & A \times G \ar[d]^{\otimes} \\
674& & A
675}
676\hspace*{1cm}
677\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
678(A\times G) \times G \ar[r]^-{\alpha_{A,G,G}} \ar[d]_{\otimes \times G}
679& A\times (G \times G) \ar[r]^-{A \times (\cdot)} & A \times G \ar[d]^{\otimes} \\
680A \times G \ar[rr]^-{\otimes} & & A
681}
682\]
683where $\rho$ and $\alpha$ are the right unital and associative laws of
684the product monoidal structure.
685But these are precisely the laws of a \emph{(right) action} of $G$ on
686$A$ (where $A$ is a uniform space, so we expect an action to also be
687uniformly continuous).
688Let us now consider coalgebra maps.
689A map
690\begin{math}
691f:(A,u)\to(B,v)
692\end{math}
693in $\coEM(D)$ is a map in $\Unif$ that commutes with $u$ and $v$ or
694(which is equivalent) with their uncurried forms $\otimes$ and
695$\oslash$ as shown on the left and right diagrams below, respectively:
696\[
697\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
698A \ar[r]^-{u} \ar[d]_{f} & A^G \ar[d]^{f^G} \\
699B \ar[r]^-{v} & B^G
700}
701\hspace*{1cm}
702\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
703A\times G \ar[r]^-{\otimes} \ar[d]_{f\times G} & A \ar[d]^{f} \\
704B\times G \ar[r]^-{\oslash} & B
705}
706\]
707Clearly, coalgebra maps are just action maps.
708We are now ready to consider maps of cofree $D$-coalgebras. The
709uncurried form of $\de_A : A^G \to (A^G)^G$ is $\rhd_A : A^G \times G
710\to A^G$. By what we have shown, a map $f : A^G \to B^G$ in $\Unif$ is
711a map between $(A^G, \de_A)$ and
712$(B^G, \de_B)$
713if and only if
714$f (c \rhd_A x) = (f (c) \rhd_B x)$.
715We see that maps between the cofree
716coalgebras $(A^G, \de_A)$ and $(B^G, \de_B)$ are precisely those maps
717$f : A^G \to B^G$ that commute with the translation!
718With our reasoning, we have reproved the version of Curtis-Hedlund
719theorem given by Ceccherini-Silberstein and Coornaert
720(\cite[Th.~1.1]{csc08}, \cite[Th.~1.9.1]{csc10}):
721global behaviors between uniform spaces $A$ and $B$ are those uniformly
722continuous functions between the product uniformities on $A^G$ and
723$B^G$ that commute with the translation.
724Keep in mind that we are allowing arbitrary uniform spaces as alphabets,
725and speaking of global behaviors in the sense of Section~\ref{sec:ca}.
726It is, however, immediate to specialize to the statement of C.-S. and C.
727by requiring $A$ and $B$ to be uniformly discrete.
728Then local behaviors are precisely
729the finitary functions from $A^G$ to $B$.
730The original Curtis-Hedlund theorem (\cite{h69},
731\cite[Th.~1.8.1]{csc10}) corresponds to the special case where $A$ is
732finite and discrete. In this case, $A^G$ is compact and
733any continuous function between $A^G$ and $B^G$ is then uniformly
734continuous. We conclude, in this case, that global behaviors between
735$A$ to $B$ are those continuous functions between the product
736topologies on $A^G$ and $B^G$ that commute with the translation.
737We have seen that the cofree coalgebra $(B^G, \delta_B : B^G \to
738(B^G)^G)$ on $B$ is the currying of the translation action $(B^G,
739\rhd_B : B^G \times G \to B^G)$. Because of the cofreeness on $B$ of
740this coalgebra, the action must also be the cofree.
741In basic terms, this
742means that
743for any action $(A, \otimes : A \times G \to A)$
744and map $p : A \to B$, there is a unique action morphism $f$
745to the translation action such that $\eps_B \circ f = p$, i.e., a map
746$f : A \to B^G$ such that the following diagrams commute:
747\[
748\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
749A \times G \ar[r]^-{\otimes} \ar@{.>}[d]_{f \times G}
750& A \ar[dr]^{p} \ar@{.>}[d]^{f}
751& \\
752B^G \times G \ar[r]^-{\rhd_B}
753& B^G \ar[r]^{\eps_B}
754& B
755}
756\]
757This fact can of course be proved from first principles, but we
758learned it for free!

760% =======================================================================
761% =======================================================================
762\section{Retrieving the reversibility principle}
763\label{sec:rev}
764We will now recover the reversibility principle. Let again $(G, 1_G,
765\cdot)$ be a monoid and $(D, \eps, \de)$ be the $G$-exponential
766comonad on $\Unif$ as introduced in Section~\ref{sec:ca}.
767Suppose we have a cofree coalgebra map $f : (D A, \de_A) \to (D B,
768\de_B)$ so that $f$ has an inverse $f^{-1}$ as a map of $\Unif$.
769A very simple diagram chase (not specific to our particular comonad;
770we only use that $D$ is a functor!) shows that $f^{-1}$ is also a
771cofree coalgebra map, i.e., an inverse of $f$ in $\coEM(D)$:
772\[
773\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
774& DA \ar[r]^-{\de_A} \ar[d]_{f}
775& D(DA) \ar[d]^{D f} \ar@{=}[r]
776& D (DA)\\
777D B \ar[ru]^{f^{-1}} \ar@{=}[r]
778& DB \ar[r]^-{\de_B}
779& D(DB) \ar[ru]_{Df^{-1}}
780&
781}
782\]
783We have thus reproved the reversibility principle
784\cite[Th.~1.10.1]{csc10}: A global behavior $f : A^G \to B^G$ (a
785uniformly continuous function commuting with the translation) between
786uniform spaces $A$, $B$ is reversible if $f$ has a uniformly
787continuous inverse.
788%(As before we do not have to require that $A$ and
789%$B$ be the same uniformly discrete space.)
790If both $A$ and $B$ are finite and discrete, an inverse $f^{-1}$ of $f$ is necessarily uniformly continuous, because, in this case, $A^G$ and $B^G$ are compact Hausdorff and $f^{-1}$ is continuous.
791So
792we obtain a special case \cite[Th.~1.10.2]{csc10}: A global behavior $f : A^G \to B^G$ (a continuous function commuting with the translation) between uniform spaces $A$, $B$ is reversible if $f$ has an inverse.
793In general, an inverse of a uniformly continuous function is not
794necessarily uniformly continuous. For a counterexample,
795see~\cite[Example 1.10.3]{csc10}.
796For reversibility, it is useful, if the monoid $G$ is actually a
797group. In particular, for reversibility of $\delta_A : D A \to D(D
798A)$, $G$ must be a group.

801% =======================================================================
802\section{Distributive laws and 2-dimensional cellular automata}
803\label{sec:2d}
804We will now proceed to two variations on the theme of cellular
805automata as co\-Kleisli maps---2-dimensional (classical) cellular
806automata and point-dependent cellular automata. In both cases we first
807introduce some further comonad theory relevant for our cause.
808Sometimes, but not always, the composition $D^1D^0$ of two comonads
809$D^0$ and $D^1$ on the same category $\C$ is a comonad. It is the
810case, if there is a distributive law of $D^1$ over $D^0$. A
811\emph{distributive law} of a comonad $(D^1, \eps^1, \de^1)$ over a
812comonad $(D^0, \eps^0, \de^0)$ is a natural transformation $\kappa :
813D^1D^0 \to D^0D^1$ making the diagrams
814\[
815\xymatrix@R=1.2pc@C=1pc{
816D^1D^0 \ar[rr]^{\kappa} \ar[dr]_{D^1 \eps^0}
817& & D^0D^1 \ar[dl]^{\eps^0 D^1} \\
818& D^1 &
819}
820\hspace*{1cm}
821\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
822D^1D^0 \ar[rr]^-{\kappa} \ar[d]_{D^1 \de^0}
823& & D^0D^1 \ar[d]^{\de^0 D^1} \\
824D^1D^0D^0 \ar[r]^-{\kappa D^0}
825& D^0D^1D^0 \ar[r]^-{D^0 \kappa}
826& D^0D^0D^1
827}
828\]
829\[
830\xymatrix@R=1.2pc@C=1pc{
831D^1D^0 \ar[rr]^{\kappa} \ar[dr]_{\eps^1 D^0}
832& & D^0D^1 \ar[dl]^{D^0 \eps^1} \\
833& D^0 &
834}
835\hspace*{1cm}
836\xymatrix@R=1.2pc{
837D^1D^0 \ar[rr]^-{\kappa} \ar[d]_{\de^1 D^0}
838& & D^0D^1 \ar[d]^{D^0 \de^1} \\
839D^1D^1D^0 \ar[r]^-{D^1 \kappa}
840& D^1D^0D^1 \ar[r]^-{\kappa D^1}
841& D^0D^1D^1
842}
843\]
844commute. A distributive law induces a comonad $(D, \eps, \de)$ defined
845by $D \eqdf D^1D^0$, $\eps \eqdf \eps^1\eps^0$, $\de \eqdf
846D^1 \kappa D^0 \comp \de^1 \de^0$.
847A distributive law also induces comonad liftings. For the lack of
848space, we concentrate on the coKleisli side of the picture. Given a
849distributive law $\kappa$ of $D^1$ over $D^0$, the comonad $D^0$ on
850$\C$ lifts to $\coKl(D^1)$, i.e., induces a comonad $\bar{D^0}$ on
851$\coKl(D^1)$. This comonad is defined by: $\bar{D^0} A \eqdf D^0 A$,
852$\bar{D^0} k \eqdf D^0 k \comp \kappa_A : D^1 D^0 A \to D^0 B$ (for $k :
853D^1 A \to B$), $\eps_A \eqdf \eps^0_A \comp \eps^1_{D^0 A}$, $\de_A
854\eqdf \de^0_A \comp \eps^1_{D^0 A}$.
855Via this lifting, the coKleisli category of the composite comonad $D$
856and the other ingredients of the coKleisli splitting of $D$ can be
857obtained by a double coKleisli construction: We have $\coKl(D) =
858\coKl(\bar{D^0})$ (equal strictly, not just isomorphic).
859A simple example of a distributive law is obtained by taking $D^1$ to
860be any comonad and $D^0$ the product comonad defined by $D^0 A \eqdf A
861\times C$ for a fixed object $C \in |\C|$. The distributive law
862$\kappa$ of $D^1$ over $D^0$ is given by $\kappa_A \eqdf \langle D^1
863\pi_0, \eps^1 \comp D^1 \pi_1 \rangle : D^1 (A\times C) \to D^1 A
864\times C$. It follows that the functor $D$ defined by $D A \eqdf D^1
865(A \times C)$ is a comonad.
866Given now two monoids $G_0$, $G_1$, we can think of a map $k :
867(A^{G_0})^{G_1} \to B$ in $\Unif$ as a ``2-dimensional'' (2D) cellular
868automaton on the universes $G_0$, $G_1$ between alphabets $A$ and $B$
869(relying on the isomorphism $A^{G_0 \times G_1} \cong
870(A^{G_0})^{G_1}$).
871Such a cellular automaton is by definition the same thing as a
872``1-dimensional'' (1D) cellular automaton on the universe $G_1$
873between alphabets $A^{G_0}$ and $B$. Note that we can only see 2D
874cellular automata as 1D in this way, if we allow source and target
875alphabets of a cellular automaton to differ and if we do not require
876them to be uniformly discrete (notice that $A^{G_0}$ carries the
877prodiscrete uniformity). But this view of 2D cellular automata as 1D,
878although nice, suffers from a serious drawback. Since the 1D views do
879not have the same source alphabets as the 2D originals, they do not
880compose the same way.
881Distributive laws come to help. Let $D^0 A \eqdf A^{G_0}$ and $D^1 A
882\eqdf A^{G_1}$.
883There is a distributive law $\kappa : D^1D^0 \to D^0D^1$ defined by $\kappa_A (c) (x_1)(x_0) = c(x_0)(x_1) : (A^{G_0})^{G_1} \to (A^{G_1})^{G_0}$.
884Hence,
885the functor $D A \eqdf (A^{G_0})^{G_1}$ is a comonad, which is hardly a surprise.
886But there is more: We know that $\coKl(D) = \coKl(\bar{D^0})$.
887Hence,
888a good view of $k : (A^{G_0})^{G_1} \to B$ as a 1D cellular automaton is not as a $\Unif$-cellular automaton on the universe $G_1$ between the alphabets $A^{G_0}$ and $B$, but on as a $\coKl(D^1)$-cellular automaton on the universe $G_0$ between the alphabets $A$ and $B$.
889Then 1D views compose exactly as their 2D originals. We see that it
890makes sense to consider maps of categories other than $\Unif$!
8911D views of 2D cellular automata were of interest to Dennuzio et
892al.~\cite{df08}

894% =======================================================================
895% =======================================================================
896\section{Comonad maps and point-dependent cellular automata}
897\label{sec:dep}
898To make a category out of comonads over a fixed category $\C$ one
899needs a suitable notion of comonad maps. A \emph{comonad map}
900between two comonads $(D, \eps, \de)$ and $(D', \eps', \de')$ on $\C$
901is a natural transformation $\tau : D \to D'$ making the diagrams
902\[
903\xymatrix@R=0.35pc{
904D \ar[rd]^-{\eps} \ar[dd]_{\tau} \\
905& \Id_\C \\
906D' \ar[ru]_-{\eps'}
907}
908\hspace*{1cm}
909\xymatrix@R=0.7pc{
910D \ar[r]^{\de} \ar[dd]_{\tau}
911& DD \ar[dd]^{\tau \tau} \\
912\\
913D' \ar[r]^-{\de'}
914& D'D'
915}
916\]
917commute. Comonads and comonad maps on $\C$ form a category. The
918identity and composition of comonad maps is inherited from the
919category of natural transformations between endofunctors on $\C$.
920A comonad map $\tau$ between $(D, \eps, \de)$ and $(D', \eps', \de')$
921relates the coKleisli and coEilenberg-Moore categories between the two
922comonads. It defines a functor from $\coKl(D')$ to $\coKl(D)$ and a
923functor from $\coEM(D)$ to $\coEM(D')$.
924We now introduce point-dependent cellular automata (studied under the
925name of non-uniform cellular automata by Cattaneo et
926al.~\cite{cdfp09}). For a set $G$, the local behavior of a
927point-dependent cellular automaton between uniform spaces $A$, $B$ is
928a uniformly continuous function $k : A^G \times G \to B$. Note the
929added second argument compared to the definition of a classical local
930behavior.
931It turns out that local and global behaviors of point-dependent
932cellular automata can be analyzed in the same way as those of
933classical cellular automata. In particular, their local behaviors are
934the same thing as coKleisli maps of a suitable comonad $(D, \eps,
935\de)$ on $\Unif$ and global behaviors are the corresponding cofree
936coalgebra maps!
937Let us review the data of the comonad. The object mapping of $D$ is
938defined by $D A \eqdf A^G \times G$ and the morphism mapping by $D f
939\eqdf f^G \times G$, i.e., $D f (c, x) \eqdf (\lambda y. f(c(y)), x)$.
940The components of the counit and comultiplication $\eps_A : A^G \times
941G \to A$ and $\de_A : A^G \times G \to (A^G \times G)^G \times G$ are
942defined by $\eps_A (c, x) \eqdf c(x)$, $\de_A (c, x) = (\lambda y.
943(c, y), x)$.
944Accordingly,
945the coKleisli extension $k^\dg : A^G \times G \to B^G \times G$ of a map $k : A^G \times G \to B$ is forced to satisfy $k^\dg (c, x) = D k (\de (c, x)) = D k (\lambda y. (c, y), x)
946= (\lambda y. k (c, y), x)$.
947When is a map $f : A^G \times G \to B^G \times G$ a global behavior?
948It is a global behavior iff it is a cofree coalgebra map. Not
949surprisingly at all, the conditions for $f$ being a cofree coalgebra
950map reduce to the condition that $f (c, x) = (g(c), x)$ for some $g :
951A^G \to B^G$.
952Assume $G$ is endowed with a monoid structure $(1_G, \cdot)$. Let
953$(D', \eps', \de')$ be the comonad of classical cellular automata.
954The translation $\rhd$ is a comonad map from $D$ to $D'$.
955Accordingly,
956any classical local behavior is also a point-dependent local behavior that simply makes no use the point information that is available.
957% =======================================================================
958% =======================================================================
959% =======================================================================
960\section{Conclusions}
961\label{sec:concl}
962It was not the purpose of this paper to prove deep or difficult
963theorems. Rather, we set out to experiment with definitions. We deem
964that this experiment succeeded. We were pleased to learn that, from
965the category-theoretic point-of-view, cellular automata are a
966``natural'' construction with ``natural'' properties. Crucially,
967classical cellular automata are coKleisli maps of the exponential
968comonad on $\Unif$, and it is harmless to accept alphabets with
969nondiscrete uniformities and variation of alphabets, once it has been
970decided that local behaviors are uniformly continuous functions. But
971other base categories can be useful too, as the example of
9722-dimensional cellular automata as 1-dimensional shows.
973We hope to be able to extend this work to cover more results of
974cellular automata theory, in particular results toward the Garden of
975Eden theorem.

977We are grateful to Jarkko Kari and Pierre Guillon for comments.
